PHSCS 587

Interface states and pinning

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how interface states change the sensitivity of a contact barrier

An ideal work-function calculation can fail when the interface contains electronic states and dipoles. Defects, bonding changes and metal-induced gap states can exchange charge with the adjoining materials. This redistribution shifts the electrostatic potential across the interface and changes the relationship between metal work function and semiconductor barrier height.

A useful empirical sensitivity is S = dφBn/dΦm, with barrier and work-function quantities expressed in the same voltage units. The ideal Schottky–Mott limit has S near one. Strong Fermi-level pinning gives a much smaller sensitivity: changing the metal has a weaker effect on the barrier. The figure compares slopes rather than assigning a universal pinned energy.

Pinning strength depends on the actual material pair, surface preparation, interfacial layers and processing. An interface-state density is commonly quoted per area per energy, such as cm⁻²eV⁻¹; its electrostatic effect also depends on occupation. Depinning strategies therefore require an interface model and measurement, rather than a work-function change alone.

Example

If a measured contact family has S = 0.15, a work-function change of 0.4 V would correspond to about 0.06 V of barrier change within that local linear fit. The fit is specific to that family and range.

Practice

1. What does a nearly horizontal barrier-versus-work-function curve indicate?

Interpret its slope S.

The barrier is weakly sensitive to the chosen metal work function, consistent with strong pinning in that contact family.
